title: Short Stuff: Feed A Cold, Starve a Fever
summary: Short Stuff episode with Josh and Chuck (Jerry sitting in for Dave) on the old saying "Feed a cold, starve a fever." They trace its origins: a 1574 dictionary by John Wilels (spelled Wile's in transcript) saying fasting is a remedy for fever, the Hippocrates reference, and the 1853 phrasing. They explain the saying was possibly read ambiguously due to a comma. They cover why medical experts consider starving a fever bad advice: appetite comes and goes, fevers raise metabolism, and hydration is essential, with calorie-containing fluids like broth and sports drinks recommended. Historical remedies from a 1785 Gentlemen's Magazine article (barley water, small beer, apple water, linseed tea, toast water) are mentioned. A 2002 Dutch study found fasting raised interleukin-4 sharply while lowering interferon-gamma, showing the immune response is not something to game by starving.

segments.title: Why starving a fever is bad advice
segments.summary: Medical consensus is that eating when hungry is advised during illness, since appetite fluctuates. Fever raises metabolism and the body needs nutrients. Hydration is essential, and calorie-containing fluids like broth and sports drinks help.

segments.title: Historical remedies and the 1785 Gentlemen's Magazine
segments.summary: Chuck cites a 1785 Gentlemen's Magazine article calling the advice destructive; it suggested barley water, small beer, apple water, linseed tea, and toast water. Small beer is explained as low-alcohol beer.

segments.title: 2002 Dutch study on fasting and immunity
segments.summary: A 2002 Dutch study fasted two groups for 24 hours; one group got a meal replacement drink. Interferon gamma rose about 450 percent in the fed group and fell about 83 percent in the fasting group, while interleukin-4 rose about 400 percent in the fasting group. The hosts conclude you cannot game the immune system and should eat when hungry.
